get.description:
Get the full result of a completed redesign job.

Served from a single builder off the authoritative DB row. A Redis result
cache used to short-circuit this read, but it was a once-per-job endpoint
whose cache was never invalidated and whose hand-maintained snapshot silently
diverged from the DB serialization (it dropped the completion-gating
``verification_status``/``verification_report`` and ``variants``), so it was
removed. There is exactly one serialization now — cache and DB cannot drift.
Download a screenshot for a specific viewport.
Download a discrete per-section redesign still by section name.

404.description: Job or section screenshot not found

post.description:
Render a self-contained HTML string to a PDF (stateless, headless Chromium print).

Unlike ``/jobs/{job_id}/pdf`` this takes the HTML in the request body instead of
loading a stored redesign job — for callers (e.g. the orchestrator audit-report
stage) that build the HTML themselves. No persistence; the bytes are streamed back.

Stateless does NOT mean anonymous. This was the only route in the module that
never resolved a tenant, so it drove unattributable Chromium work — a full
browser engine, on caller-supplied markup, inside the cluster — for anyone who
could reach the port. ``_get_tenant_id`` fails closed with a 401, so the work
is authenticated and attributable like every sibling route even though there is
no row to scope. The orchestrator already sends ``X-Tenant-Id`` on this call
(``BaseServiceClient``), so nothing legitimate loses access.

get.description:
List all custom styles for the tenant, deactivated ones included.

A MANAGEMENT listing, like ``GET /styles/{id}``: every row carries
``is_active`` so a client can filter for itself. It must show deactivated
rows because ``count_styles`` charges quota for them — an active-only list
would let a tenant hit "maximum custom styles reached" on ``POST`` while
``GET`` reported ``count: 0``, with no way left to obtain the ``style_id``
that ``PUT`` (to reactivate) and ``DELETE`` (to free the slot) both require.
That was a permanent, API-inescapable lockout.

delete.description:
Delete a custom style.

Reads the row first — with ``include_inactive`` so a deactivated style is
still deletable — purely to learn its ``slug``: the cache key is
``(tenant_id, slug)`` and after the DELETE there is nothing left to derive it
from. The DELETE keeps its own tenant predicate (it is not relying on this
read for scoping); the read only turns a miss into the same 404 as before.

get.description:
Get a custom style by ID.

A MANAGEMENT read: it opts into deactivated styles (``include_inactive``)
because the response body carries ``is_active`` precisely so the owner can
see and manage a switched-off style. Hiding it here while ``PUT`` can still
reactivate it — and while it still occupies a quota slot — would leave the
row invisible but chargeable.

put.description:
Update a custom style.

Both reads opt into deactivated styles: this is the ONLY route that can flip
``is_active`` back to True, so filtering them out here would strand a
deactivated row permanently (404 on its own guard) while it still consumed a
quota slot.

post.description:
Preview a custom style applied to an HTML snippet.

A CONSUMPTION route, not a management one: it renders the style, exactly as
the generation path does. So it takes the default active-only ``get_style``
and now 404s on a deactivated style, matching ``get_style_by_slug`` — which
every real redesign/variant/refinement lookup goes through. Previously this
was the one place a switched-off style still produced output (and still spent
an LLM call).

get.description:
Combined health check for all components.

Reports the two components that actually do the work — the claim-queue worker
tasks and the Chromium pool — alongside the DB/Redis dependencies. Neither is
wired into readiness; see :func:`health_ready` for why.
Kubernetes liveness probe.

Kubernetes readiness probe -- checks database connectivity.

The worker pool and the browser pool are deliberately NOT checked here, and
that is a decision, not an omission:

* **Readiness gates HTTP, but work does not arrive over HTTP.** Jobs are
  *pulled* off a shared Postgres claim queue, not pushed by the Service. So
  evicting a pod whose workers died stops none of the damage — it only
  removes a submit/status/artifact surface that is still perfectly correct.
* **The realistic causes are shared, not per-pod.** A bad image or config
  kills the workers on every replica at once. Readiness would then evict all
  of them simultaneously, so on top of a stalled queue clients could no
  longer submit jobs or poll the ones already queued. That is strictly worse
  than the blindness it replaces.
* **Liveness was considered and rejected** for the same reason: a restart
  would fix a locally-crashed pool, but a shared cause turns it into a
  fleet-wide crashloop.

So the signal lands on ``/health`` as ``status: unhealthy`` — loud to an
operator and to alerting, inert to the scheduler.
Modern K8s liveness probe path (alias of /health/live).
Modern K8s readiness probe path (alias of /health/ready).
